R1.title: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other
R1.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R1.evidence_summary: The first and last steps are well supported: L01: Concentrated wealth funds more political spending rests on donor records, and L03: Policy advantages add to wealth at the top on CBO's accounting of who receives tax benefits. The middle step, L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors, is plausible and the weakest. A 2016 field experiment found that donors get meetings, and since affluent and middle-income Americans want the same policy about 90% of the time, any tilt shows only where they disagree.
R1.how_to_read: Concentration of household wealth raises money spent to influence politics, which raises policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, which in turn raise the concentration of household wealth.
R1.summary: Households with concentrated wealth can spend more on campaigns, outside groups and lobbying. That spending can win rules, such as low tax rates on investment income, that add to wealth at the top. The added wealth pays for the next round of spending.
R1.qualification: The loop runs on issues where wealthy donors' preferences differ from those of middle-income voters; on most issues the two groups agree, so its reach depends on the issue.
R1.reference_mode: Top 1% wealth share 22.8% (1989) to 32.5% (2026Q2, a record)

R1b.title: Political spending and court rulings reinforce each other
R1b.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R1b.evidence_summary: L05: Court rulings widen permitted political spending is documented in decisions from Buckley v. Valeo (1976) to NRSC v. FEC (2026). The weakest step is L04: Political money helps shape judicial confirmations, graded plausible: the cited work is a history of organized legal movements (Teles 2008), with no estimate of how much money changes confirmations.
R1b.how_to_read: Money spent to influence politics raises court rulings favoring the appointing coalition, which raise the money spent to influence politics.
R1b.summary: Money spent on politics pays for confirmation campaigns and test cases that shape which judges sit and which questions they hear. Those judges set the legal limits on political spending. Wider limits let more money into the next round.
R1b.qualification: The doctrine variable has no published scoring rule and is read through named decisions, and nothing in the evidence ties a donation to a particular ruling.

R2.title: Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise
R2.evidence_summary: Both steps are hypotheses. L18: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence draws on studies of reliance on lobbyists (Drutman 2015) and on model bills in state legislatures (Hertel-Fernandez 2019). The return step, L19: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise, is the weakest, since it rests on a single event: the 1995 staff cuts.
R2.how_to_read: Congress's ability to write and check policy lowers policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, and those advantages lower Congress's ability to write and check policy; two negative steps make the loop reinforcing.
R2.summary: When Congress cuts its own analysts, members and committees lean on analysis supplied by interested industries. Policy drafted that way can tilt toward those industries. Rules that favor them can weaken support for rebuilding public expertise.
R2.qualification: Staff losses and lobbying totals are documented, and neither step has been tested, so the loop is a proposed explanation for the pattern.

R3.title: Political hostility and hostile content may reinforce each other
R3.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R3.evidence_summary: L46: Hostility increases demand for hostile content is plausible, and its supply side rests on internal messages released in Dominion v. Fox (2023). The return step, L47: Hostile content may raise partisan hostility slightly, is contested and the weakest. Randomized feed experiments in 2020 and 2023 changed exposure a great deal and found precisely estimated null effects on partisan hostility, while a 2024 reranking test moved out-party warmth about 2 points on a 0 to 100 scale.
R3.how_to_read: Hostility toward the other political party raises exposure to hostile political content, which raises hostility toward the other political party.
R3.summary: People who dislike the other party seek out and share posts that attack it, and outlets and platforms supply more of them. Exposure to those posts may then raise hostility slightly. The proposed loop asks whether the two feed each other over time.
R3.qualification: Measured effects of exposure on hostility are small. A 2026 study of X (Gauthier and coauthors) found the feed algorithm moved users' policy priorities about a tenth of a standard deviation toward conservative positions with no effect on partisan hostility; policy views are a separate outcome from hostility.

R4a.title: Majorities draw maps that help them keep control
R4a.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R4a.evidence_text: documented for C4 to C1 and D7 to C4; plausible for C1 to D7
R4a.evidence_summary: Two steps are documented by the 2025 to 2026 mid-decade redraws: L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats and L56: Durable majorities control maps and voting rules. The weakest is L55: Safe seats keep majorities in power, graded plausible, because seat safety is documented while its effect on how long majorities last rests on seats-votes analysis without a single estimate.
R4a.how_to_read: Officeholders' control over election rules raises the number of seats with little electoral competition, which raises entrenched control of rule-setting institutions, which raises officeholders' control over election rules.
R4a.summary: A legislative majority draws district maps that make many of its seats safe. With most seats safe, swings in the popular vote flip few seats, so the majority holds on. Holding on lets it draw the next map.
R4a.qualification: Courts and voters can interrupt the loop, as in Missouri, where the 2025 map is set aside for 2026 pending a November 3 referendum. Voters' residential sorting also makes seats safe without any map.
R4a.reference_mode: Share of seats decided by over 10 points, 1992 to 2024

R4b.title: Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable
R4b.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R4b.evidence_summary: L44: Restrictive access rules widen turnout gaps is well supported for registration barriers, though voter ID laws showed effects near zero (Cantoni and Pons 2021). The return step, L45: Broad turnout makes entrenchment harder, is plausible and the weaker of the two; it rests on comparisons across states (Grumbach 2022).
R4b.how_to_read: Officeholders' control over election rules lowers the equality of voter turnout, and less equal turnout raises officeholders' control over election rules; two negative steps make the loop reinforcing.
R4b.summary: Officeholders who control election rules can make registering or voting harder. Turnout then falls most among the groups facing the highest costs, and the electorate becomes less equal. A narrower electorate is easier to hold power against.
R4b.qualification: Effects differ by rule and by state, so the existence of a restriction does not establish its size or which party gains from it.

R5.title: Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions
R5.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R5.evidence_summary: L35: Financial security makes turnout more equal is well supported (Schlozman, Verba and Brady 2012), and so is L37: Insider-tilted benefit rules reduce household security, through Census poverty data on benefits that expired. The middle step, L36: More equal turnout reduces policy favoritism, is plausible and the weakest: its main evidence is Australia's adoption of compulsory voting in the early 20th century (Fowler 2013).
R5.how_to_read: Households' financial security raises the equality of voter turnout; more equal turnout lowers policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, and those advantages lower households' financial security.
R5.summary: Households under financial strain have less time and money to spare for voting and public meetings. With turnout unequal, officeholders respond more to those who vote, and rules tilt toward wealthier and organized interests. Rules of that kind, such as letting a benefit lapse, leave struggling households with even less room.
R5.qualification: Time, money and civic skills each affect turnout, and the evidence does not support treating lack of free time as the single cause.

R6.title: Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other
R6.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R6.evidence_text: well-supported for A2 to A1; plausible for the rest
R6.evidence_summary: L30: Worker bargaining power limits top wealth concentration and L01: Concentrated wealth funds more political spending are well supported. The political steps are plausible: L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors carries the limits described for loop R1, and L31: Insider-tilted labor rules weaken worker bargaining rests on legal events from the Taft-Hartley Act (1947) to the labor board's period without a quorum in 2025. The weakest is L02.
R6.how_to_read: Workers' bargaining power lowers the concentration of household wealth; that concentration raises money spent to influence politics, which raises policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, which lower workers' bargaining power.
R6.summary: When workers have less bargaining power, more of the income from production goes to owners, and wealth concentrates. Concentrated wealth funds political spending that can tilt labor law and its enforcement. Weaker labor rules leave workers with even less bargaining power.
R6.qualification: The bargaining-to-wealth step comes from studies of income inequality, and wealth also moves with asset prices; the political steps that close the loop share the limits of loop R1.

R7.title: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other
R7.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R7.evidence_text: hypothesis for the named direction; plausible for the compliance channel; the delivery leg is documented case by case in the Delivery Log, though no study measures the loop closing
R7.evidence_summary: Both steps are graded plausible. In L20: Better public services build earned trust, survey trust also moves with which party holds office (Hetherington 2005). L21: Earned trust supports compliance and service funding works through compliance and revenue, which tax morale research supports; its funding channel is a hypothesis and the weakest part of the loop.
R7.how_to_read: The quality of public services raises trust earned through performance, which raises the quality of public services.
R7.summary: When a public service works, the people who use it gain a reason to trust the agency. Trust supports compliance and tax revenue, which help keep the service working. Run in reverse, a failing service loses trust and with it the support it needs.
R7.qualification: No study has measured the complete loop, and the claim that a service failure makes the next budget cut easier is a hypothesis.

R-01.title: All-party primaries with ranked general elections
R-01.summary: Every voter, whatever their party, could vote in one first-round election, and two or more candidates would advance to a November ballot that all voters use. In seats that one party usually wins, the choice now made in a low-turnout party primary would move to the full electorate. In Massachusetts, unenrolled voters already pick one party's ballot. Under Question 3, every voter would see all candidates on one primary ballot from 2028. The Atlas takes no position on Question 3 or Ballot Measure 2.
R-01.remedy_text: More contested general elections and more candidates entering races are plausible results. Whether legislators become more moderate is contested: a 2014 study of state legislators by McGhee and colleagues found that more open primaries had little consistent effect on ideology, and experimental work finds that primary effects depend on conditions. Main limitation: Alaska's top-four system has a short record, so there is no long-run U.S. test of a top-four primary paired with a ranked general election.
R-01.what_it_changes: In a safe seat the general election is predictable, so the party primary picks the winner (L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive). That weakens the threat incumbents face from the wider public (L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure). An all-party primary sends more than one candidate to November, which aims to lower C2: How often the primary decides the winner and raise C3: Risk of losing office. A top-two design advances two candidates; a top-four design advances four and can be paired with a ranked-choice general election. The reform sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates), loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance) and loop R11 (Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms).

R-02.title: Ranked-choice voting for single-winner races
R-02.summary: Voters would rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins more than half of the first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots count for each voter's next choice, round by round. Voters who back minor-party or independent candidates would gain at the first ranked election, because a first choice for a long shot would stop helping elect the candidate they like least.
R-02.remedy_text: Evidence that ranking improves campaign civility and voter understanding is moderate. Evidence that it raises turnout or produces more moderate winners is weak. Main limitation: some ballots drop out of the count. A 2015 study of four local ranked elections found that 9.6% to 27.1% of ballots ranked no candidate still in the final round, so winners often lacked a majority of all ballots cast.
R-02.what_it_changes: Under plurality voting, two similar candidates can split their supporters and let a third candidate win; this is called the spoiler problem. Ranking removes that penalty, so more candidates can run, and it rewards candidates who seek second-choice support from other camps. The reform is linked to C3: Risk of losing office and to variable B4: Hostility toward the other political party. It sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).

R-03.title: Proportional elections in multi-seat House districts
R-03.summary: Larger House districts would each elect several members, with seats shared in proportion to votes. Voters who support the minority party in a one-party region could elect someone at the first election under the new map, and incumbents in safe seats would face more competition. Small states with one or two seats would see little change.
R-03.remedy_text: Support comes from comparisons across countries and from simulations. Carey and Hix (2011) found in cross-national data that districts electing three to eight members improve proportionality without fragmenting governments. Main limitation: no U.S. congressional election has used the system, so there is no direct American test.
R-03.what_it_changes: Single-member districts let maps and the way voters cluster geographically produce safe seats (L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats). With several seats per district and a proportional count, most seats become contestable and the majority tracks the vote. The aim is to lower C1: Seats with little electoral competition and D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions, even where geography sorts voters. The reform acts on loop R4a (Majorities draw maps that help them keep control), loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates) and loop R12 (Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules).
