R-04.title: Independent citizen commissions draw election maps
R-04.summary: A commission independent of the legislative majority would draw district maps under explicit criteria, with public hearings. Voters who support a state's minority party would see fairer maps at the next redistricting, due in 2031 after the census, unless a mid-decade redraw comes first. The legislative majority would lose the power to draw its own districts.
R-04.remedy_text: Evidence that commissions reduce partisan bias comes from one descriptive study of the 2021-22 maps: Warshaw, McGhee and Migurski found less partisan bias in commission-drawn and court-drawn maps than in legislature-drawn ones. Evidence that commissions create more competitive seats is weaker. Main limitation: that study covers one redistricting cycle and uses descriptive measures.
R-04.what_it_changes: A durable majority can use its hold on the legislature to draw maps and set access rules (L56: Durable majorities control maps and voting rules), and those maps produce safe seats (L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats). A commission cuts the step from D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions to C4: Officeholders' control over election rules. It works through loop R4a (Majorities draw maps that help them keep control).

R-05.title: Automatic voter registration
R-05.summary: Eligible people would be registered to vote when they deal with a state agency, such as the motor vehicle office or a benefits office, unless they opt out. Renters, people who move often and young adults would gain at the next election after the system starts, because a registration step that falls hardest on them would be handled for them.
R-05.remedy_text: Registration rises where the policy is adopted: a 2019 Brennan Center for Justice analysis of seven early-adopting states found registration gains of 9% to 94% after adjusting for trends. Effects on turnout are small but positive. Main limitation: that analysis measured registration, so the turnout finding comes from separate research.
R-05.what_it_changes: Registration rules can lower turnout among the people they burden (L44: Restrictive access rules widen turnout gaps). Automatic registration removes one such cost. It aims to raise B5: Equality of voter turnout, where a smaller turnout gap between income groups counts as an increase. It operates on loop R4b (Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable).

R-06.title: Hold local elections alongside November races
R-06.summary: City and county elections would move to the same November ballot as state and national races. Turnout in local contests would rise at the first combined election, and younger voters and renters would make up more of the electorate. Groups that do well when few people vote would lose some influence over local decisions on zoning, schools and contracts.
R-06.remedy_text: Using California voter files, Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian (2022) found that on-cycle timing roughly doubles turnout and makes the local electorate more representative. A school-district study by Kogan, Lavertu and Peskowitz (2018) found that off-cycle timing shifted the electorate and raised teacher pay relative to on-cycle districts, which links timing to policy. Main limitation: effects on housing and other policy outcomes are plausible but less established than the turnout effect.
R-06.what_it_changes: Off-cycle local elections draw small electorates that are older and more often homeowners. Moving them to November changes who votes. The aim is to raise B5: Equality of voter turnout and to weaken L39: Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing, since homeowners tend to fill the zoning room. The reform touches loop R8 (Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building), loop R15 (Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other), loop R16 (Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).

R-07.title: Public matching for small donations and vouchers
R-07.summary: Candidates who join a voluntary program would receive public money that multiplies small donations, or voters would receive vouchers to give to the candidates they choose. Candidates without wealthy networks would gain in the first election cycle, because small donors would become worth their time. Incumbents who rely on large-donor networks would lose ground over several cycles.
R-07.remedy_text: Evidence concerns donor participation and candidate entry, where effects are plausible. Kilborn and Vishwanath (2022) found that public matching does not make elected officials more moderate. Main limitation: direct effects on the wealth-and-policy loop are unproven.
R-07.what_it_changes: Public matching or vouchers change who funds campaigns (B1: Money spent to influence politics) and widen who can afford to run, which works on C3: Risk of losing office through more challengers. It touches loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance). Its target is candidate entry. Evidence does not show that it weakens loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other).

R-08.title: Disclose the original funders of political spending
R-08.summary: Groups that spend money to influence elections would have to report who paid, including money passed through other organizations. Voters and journalists would see that information from the first reporting deadline after the law takes effect. Groups that now spend without naming their funders would lose that option.
R-08.remedy_text: Studies find no measurable chilling effect of disclosure on donors, and moderate evidence that knowing the funder changes how persuasive voters find a message. Main limitation: disclosure works only when an agency can enforce it, which is the gap at the federal level today.
R-08.what_it_changes: Political spending can buy access and influence over policy (L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors, rated plausible). Disclosure lets voters and enforcers see who pays. That strengthens oversight's ability to catch favoritism (L16: Watchdogs reduce favoritism and waste in policy) and turns donor influence into a political cost. The reform acts on loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other), loop R3 (Political hostility and hostile content may reinforce each other) and loop B1a (Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism).

R-09.title: Ban stock trading by members of Congress
R-09.summary: Members of Congress would be barred from trading individual stocks, which removes a conflict between their own investments and their votes. The change would apply once enacted. Members who trade would lose that option, and the expected gain in public confidence has not been measured.
R-09.remedy_text: No federal ban has been tested, so its effect on members' behavior is unknown. An effect on public trust is plausible. Main limitation: trust surveys capture many influences, so a change after enactment would be hard to attribute to this rule.
R-09.what_it_changes: The reform removes one documented conflict between members' personal finances and their votes. The reform is linked to E1: Policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests and to E2: Trust earned through performance, and sits on loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other). Whether spouses and other family members are covered is a key design choice, since trading by family members is the expected workaround.

R-10.title: Limits on lobbying and the revolving door
R-10.summary: Former officials would face waiting periods before lobbying the offices they left, and lobbying disclosure would cover more of the people who do influence work. Public-interest advocates would gain over several years as insider access loses value. Former officials who lobby would lose some of the value of their connections once the law takes effect.
R-10.remedy_text: Evidence that cooling-off periods change behavior is weak. Main limitation: unregistered influence work is hard to observe, so studies can miss the activity the rules target.
R-10.what_it_changes: Lobbyists with personal ties to officials command a premium for access. Limits on the revolving door, the movement of people between public office and lobbying jobs, reduce what that access is worth. The reform is linked to L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors and to the proposed loop R2 (Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise), whose links L18: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence and L19: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise are rated hypotheses.

R-11.title: A Federal Election Commission able to act
R-11.summary: The Federal Election Commission, which enforces federal campaign-finance law, would regain enough commissioners to make decisions and work through its backlog. Candidates harmed by violations would gain as soon as a quorum returns, and violators would lose the cover of an agency that cannot act. A later step would redesign the commission so its independence can survive recent court rulings.
R-11.remedy_text: The case for a working commission rests on design lessons drawn from state election commissions. Main limitation: no study measures how quickly enforcement recovers after a quorum returns, and each structural redesign carries its own risk of partisan control.
R-11.what_it_changes: Without a quorum, no federal rule on election money is enforced. Restoring the referee raises D4: Ability to investigate and enforce the rules. The commission's quorum loss is one of the documented cases under L14: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies, and a working commission lets L15: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action operate again. The reform works through loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other) and loop R18 (Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action).

R-12.title: Senate filibuster reform
R-12.summary: A majority of the Senate could pass ordinary bills without first gathering 60 votes to end debate. Whichever party holds the majority would gain that power right away, and the minority would lose its ability to block. More laws could pass, and policy could swing further each time control changes.
R-12.remedy_text: Majority passage would raise the number of laws enacted. Main limitation: the net effect on democratic quality is uncertain, because faster lawmaking can also mean larger reversals when control changes.
R-12.what_it_changes: When Congress cannot pass laws, presidents fill the gap with executive action (L11: A weaker Congress invites presidential action), and that reliance can weaken Congress further (L12: Presidential action erodes Congress's will to legislate). Letting a majority pass statutes aims to raise D1: Congress's ability to write and check policy. It operates on loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).

R-13.title: Rebuild Congress's own staff and experts
R-13.summary: Congress would hire and keep more of its own analysts, on committees and at support agencies such as the Congressional Research Service, the Congressional Budget Office and the Government Accountability Office. Committees and the public would gain within two to four years, as members depend less on lobbyists to draft and assess bills. Lobbyists who now draft legislation would lose part of that role.
R-13.remedy_text: That more staff raise Congress's capacity is plausible. The full feedback loop, in which thin staffing leads to policy that favors insiders and then to further cuts, is a hypothesis. Main limitation: no study measures that loop from start to finish.
R-13.what_it_changes: In-house experts let members judge proposals without relying on interested parties. Link L18: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence and its return link L19: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise are both rated hypotheses; together they form the proposed loop R2 (Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise). The reform also raises D1: Congress's ability to write and check policy.

routes.who: Chamber rules on staff pay and roles

R-14.title: Automatic funding to prevent government shutdowns
R-14.summary: If Congress missed a budget deadline, funding would continue at the prior year's level until a new spending law passed, so government services would keep running. Federal workers, contractors and people who rely on federal services would gain at the next lapse that would otherwise have closed offices. The threat of a shutdown would stop working as a bargaining tool.
R-14.remedy_text: Support comes from design analysis. Main limitation: the federal government has never run under an automatic continuing resolution, so there is no U.S. test.
R-14.what_it_changes: A continuing resolution is a temporary law that keeps funding at prior levels. Making one automatic shields D5: Quality of public services from shutdowns. The reform sits on loop R7 (Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other). A shutdown documents a service failure; the later steps of that loop, from failure to lower trust to lower funding, need their own evidence.

R-15.title: Inspectors general with remedies that work
R-15.summary: Inspectors general, the internal watchdogs in federal agencies, would gain remedies that work when an administration obstructs them: reinstatement after unlawful removal, access to records, protected budgets and timely enforcement of subpoenas. Taxpayers and the public would gain over years as investigations continue under pressure. Officials under investigation would lose the ability to stall them, starting immediately.
R-15.remedy_text: The value of oversight is documented. Main limitation: new protections may not last, because their reach after the Slaughter decision is legally uncertain.
R-15.what_it_changes: When the executive removes watchdogs or cuts their resources, detection weakens (L14: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies). Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action (L15: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action) and find and correct favoritism and waste (L16: Watchdogs reduce favoritism and waste in policy). The reform aims to keep D4: Ability to investigate and enforce the rules working. It touches loop B1a (Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism) and loop R18 (Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action).

R-16.title: Supreme Court 18-year terms and enforceable ethics
R-16.summary: Supreme Court justices would serve regular 18-year terms, giving each presidential term two appointments, and the Court's ethics code would gain a process for enforcing it. Over decades, the Court's makeup would follow elections at a steady pace, and the timing of deaths and retirements would matter less. Whichever coalition the Court now favors would lose that edge gradually.
R-16.remedy_text: Support comes from simulations of how regular terms would change the Court's makeup. Main limitation: no such system has been tried, so there is no test.
R-16.what_it_changes: Appointments now depend on when vacancies occur, and a durable Senate majority with the presidency decides who is confirmed (L57: Durable Senate majorities shape court appointments). Regular terms aim to steady D3: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition, a proposed pattern assessed decision by decision. The reform acts on loop R1b (Political spending and court rulings reinforce each other) and loop R12 (Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules). Fixed terms for justices differ from legislative term limits (R-35), a rejected option.

R-17.title: Protect the career civil service
R-17.summary: Federal agencies would hire on merit and protect career employees from being fired for political reasons, keeping experienced staff in place. People who rely on agency services, such as tax help and Social Security, would gain within two to five years as staffing and expertise recover. Political leadership would lose some control over who serves in policy roles, starting immediately.
R-17.remedy_text: Aneja and Xu (2024) found that civil-service reform under the 1883 Pendleton Act cut postal delivery errors by about 20% in U.S. cities, mainly by reducing staff turnover after elections. Rauch and Evans (2000), studying 35 developing countries, found merit-based recruitment to be the feature of bureaucracies most associated with better performance ratings. Main limitation: both studies are historical or cross-national, and protections need performance management alongside them.
R-17.what_it_changes: Experienced career staff raise D5: Quality of public services. Better services can build trust (L20: Better public services build earned trust), and trust supports the compliance and funding that services need (L21: Earned trust supports compliance and service funding). The reform works through loop R7 (Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other) and loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).

routes.who: Codify protections and reverse Schedule Policy/Career

R-18.title: Expiring emergency powers and enforced spending law
R-18.summary: National emergencies declared by a president would end after a set period unless Congress voted to renew them, and the law against withholding money Congress has appropriated would be enforced on time. Congress would regain authority by default once the law took effect. Presidents would lose some room to act alone, and responses to a real emergency could be slower.
R-18.remedy_text: Cross-national evidence on emergency powers supports time limits. Main limitation: substitution under other statutes can blunt any single limit, as the 2026 tariff case showed.
R-18.what_it_changes: Emergencies expand presidential power and rarely retract fully (LX5: Emergencies expand presidential power), and a weaker Congress leaves room for presidential action (L11: A weaker Congress invites presidential action). Tariffs show how this works: presidents set them under statutes that delegate power (LE19: The executive sets tariff rates). Sunsets return delegated power to Congress unless it acts again, which aims to limit D2: Presidential action without new legislation. Enforcing the law against impoundment, the withholding of appropriated funds, protects Congress's spending decisions. The reform operates on loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).

routes.who: Emergency sunset statute (ARTICLE ONE Act model)

R-19.title: Rules for drug-pricing middlemen (PBMs)
R-19.summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), the companies that manage drug benefits for insurers and employers, would face rules that cut conflicts in how they earn money, such as rebates tied to list prices and steering patients to pharmacies they own. Patients with high out-of-pocket drug costs would gain from 2028, when key federal provisions take effect. PBMs that share owners with insurers and pharmacies would lose some revenue.
R-19.remedy_text: Separating PBM pay from list prices has not been tested at scale. Main limitation: if rebates fall, insurance premiums could shift, so savings to patients need monitoring.
R-19.what_it_changes: Concentration among a few middlemen (A3: Market concentration) can raise what patients and plans pay for drugs, part of EC9: Cost of essentials. Breaking the conflicts aims to let savings reach patients and plans. The reform touches loop B3 (New competitors can limit market power).

R-20.title: Merger enforcement for consumers and workers
R-20.summary: Antitrust agencies would block or unwind mergers that raise prices for buyers or lower wages for workers, keeping a second bidder in each market. Consumers and workers in affected markets would gain over years. Companies seeking such deals would lose them at review.
R-20.remedy_text: Blocking harmful mergers plausibly protects prices and wages, while evidence on productivity effects is weak. Main limitation: winning a case differs from changing a market, so outcomes need follow-up study.
R-20.what_it_changes: When a few firms control a market, they can raise prices and, as employers, hold down pay (L29: Employer concentration lowers workers' bargaining power). Concentration may also lower workers' share of income (LE06: Market concentration lowers workers' income share, rated contested). Merger enforcement aims to keep A3: Market concentration in check, and it acts on loop B3 (New competitors can limit market power).

R-21.title: Faster labor-law remedies and first-contract arbitration
R-21.summary: Workers fired illegally for organizing would get faster and stronger remedies. When a new union and an employer cannot agree on a first contract, a neutral arbitrator would set the terms. Workers trying to organize would gain over several years, and employers that resist organizing would face higher costs.
R-21.effects_confidence: high (FCA stoppages); medium (first contracts, density link); low (density response)
R-21.remedy_text: In Canadian provinces with first-contract arbitration, Johnson (2010) found fewer work stoppages over first contracts and more settlements, with variation across provinces. Main limitation: the evidence comes from Canada, so U.S. effects and implementation still need assessment.
R-21.what_it_changes: Weak labor law and slow enforcement reduce what workers can win at the bargaining table (L31: Insider-tilted labor rules weaken worker bargaining). Penalties that deter illegal firings, and arbitration that produces a first contract, aim to raise A2: Workers' bargaining power. Where workers can bargain, more of each dollar of output goes to wages (LE05: Bargaining power raises workers' share). The reform works through loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other) and loop R15 (Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other).

R-22.title: Industry-wide wage boards and sector bargaining
R-22.summary: Boards with worker and employer representatives would set wage and safety floors for a whole industry, such as fast food or nursing homes, so standards would not depend on organizing one workplace at a time. Covered workers would gain when the first standard takes effect. Employers in the sector would see narrower margins, and evidence on job and price effects is disputed.
R-22.remedy_text: Evidence is contested. Two studies of California's $20 fast-food minimum wage, set under the state's 2023 Fast Food Council law (AB 1228), disagree on its effects on jobs and prices; an early evaluation by Reich at UC Berkeley reported no detectable job loss. Main limitation: these are early studies of one state and one sector.
R-22.what_it_changes: Bargaining one workplace at a time covers few U.S. workers. Sector boards set floors across an industry, so competitors cannot undercut a covered workplace. The aim is to raise A2: Workers' bargaining power and EC3: Workers' share of income. The reform operates on loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other).

R-23.title: Minimum wage that rises with an index
R-23.summary: The minimum wage would rise each year with a published measure of prices or wages, so the lowest-paid workers would keep pace between legislative votes. Low-wage workers would gain as the new floor phases in. Low-margin employers would bear higher labor costs over the same period.
R-23.effects_confidence: high to 60% of median; low above
R-23.remedy_text: Within studied ranges, evidence finds little job loss. Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer (2019), studying state increases through 2016, found no detectable job loss, a result other methods dispute. The evidence is strongest up to about 60% of the local median wage. Main limitation: higher floors fall outside the studied range; the Congressional Budget Office's 2019 median estimate for a $15 federal floor by 2025 was 1.3 million jobs lost and 1.3 million people lifted from poverty, with wide uncertainty.
R-23.what_it_changes: An indexed floor raises pay at the bottom without a new legislative vote every few years. It aims to raise EC7: Household income and A4: Households' financial security, and it touches loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other).

R-24.title: Paid family and medical leave insurance
R-24.summary: Workers would receive part of their pay while they take time off for their own illness, a new child or a sick family member, paid for by payroll contributions. Workers with new children or sick relatives would gain once benefits begin, a year after contributions start. Employers would pay contributions from the start.
R-24.remedy_text: Leave-taking rises under these programs: an early study of California's program found more leave and later more work hours among mothers. Long-run employment effects are contested; a later California study found lower employment and earnings for first-time mothers. Main limitation: most evidence comes from one state's program.
R-24.what_it_changes: Caring for family takes time and money (EC9: Cost of essentials), and losing a job to provide care weakens A4: Households' financial security. Paid leave insurance pays for time to give care without losing the job. It acts on loop R5 (Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions).

R-25.title: Full child tax credit for low-earning families
R-25.summary: Families would receive the full child tax credit even if they earn little or nothing, because the credit would be fully refundable, paid out even when it exceeds the tax a family owes. Low-income families with children would gain from the first payment. Federal taxpayers would bear the cost each year, about $100 billion at the 2021 design.
R-25.remedy_text: The poverty effect of the credit is large and well supported, and a 2019 National Academies review found that income support improves child outcomes. The effect on parents' employment is contested. Main limitation: the 2021 expansion lasted one year, so direct evidence on a permanent program is limited to that short period.
R-25.what_it_changes: Benefits paid through the tax system lift households above the poverty line (LE14: Public benefits lift households out of poverty). A credit paid in full to families with little or no earnings raises EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits, where a higher value means more net support for the households discussed, and A4: Households' financial security. The reform works through loop R5 (Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions) and loop B2 (Automatic benefits cushion economic shocks).

R-26.title: Recession aid that starts automatically
R-26.summary: Benefits such as unemployment insurance would expand automatically when published measures, such as rising unemployment, show a downturn, so help would arrive without waiting for Congress to agree on a new bill. Workers who lose jobs or hours in the next recession would gain. In good years the cost would be zero.
R-26.remedy_text: The stabilizing effect of benefits that expand in downturns is well supported. Main limitation: trigger design and delivery systems decide whether help arrives on time and reaches the right people.
R-26.what_it_changes: Benefits written into law that grow as conditions worsen help households absorb a shock while Congress considers more (loop B2: Automatic benefits cushion economic shocks). Building triggers into law aims to raise EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits during downturns and to protect A4: Households' financial security.

R-27.title: IRS enforcement of taxes already owed
R-27.summary: The IRS would get steady, multi-year funding to hire and train auditors for complex, high-income returns, with taxpayer rights protected. Taxpayers who already comply would gain over years as more of the tax owed is collected. High-income people who underpay would face a higher chance of audit.
R-27.remedy_text: Using IRS data, Boning, Hendren, Sprung-Keyser and Stuart estimate that an added $1 spent auditing taxpayers above the 90th income percentile returns more than $12 in revenue, against about $5 for taxpayers below the median. Main limitation: returns fall as enforcement spending grows, and lasting gains depend on durable funding and fair treatment of taxpayers.
R-27.what_it_changes: Tax law already steers many benefits to the top (LE12: Insider-tilted tax law reduces net household support), and weak enforcement widens the gap between the rules as written and what is paid. Auditing high-income returns collects tax owed and acts on E1: Policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests. A better-staffed IRS also improves D5: Quality of public services, such as phone service. The reform operates on loop R7 (Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other).

R-28.title: Taxing inherited gains and capital income
R-28.summary: Gains on stocks, businesses and other assets would be taxed when their owner dies, and income from capital would be taxed more like wages. Future taxpayers would gain over decades as revenue rises and the largest fortunes grow more slowly. Large estates would pay more at the owner's death.
R-28.remedy_text: Calibrated economic models support the direction. Natural experiments with wealth taxes in Denmark and Switzerland found that taxing wealth reduces its measured accumulation at the top, partly through avoidance. Main limitation: that evidence concerns wealth taxes in other countries, and illiquid family businesses need explicit rules.
R-28.what_it_changes: Tax preferences for capital income help large fortunes grow (L03: Policy advantages add to wealth at the top). Under a rule called step-up in basis, gains on assets held until death escape income tax when heirs inherit them. Ending step-up and taxing capital income more like wages aims to slow the growth of A1: Concentration of household wealth and EC4: Concentration of stock ownership. The reform touches loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other).

R-29.title: Baby bonds: publicly funded child accounts
R-29.summary: Children would receive a publicly funded savings account early in life, with larger deposits for children from families with little wealth. Children born into families without wealth would gain at 18, when they can use the money. The main benefit arrives 18 years after the program starts.
R-29.remedy_text: The arithmetic is strong: money deposited early grows by adulthood. An Oklahoma randomized experiment with universal child accounts (SEED OK) found modest gains in young children's social and emotional development. Main limitation: how families use and add to accounts at national scale is untested, and long-run outcomes are unknown.
R-29.what_it_changes: Family wealth shapes what young adults own and owe (EC8: Household assets and debts). Accounts seeded early give children without family wealth an asset at adulthood. The reform acts on loop R5 (Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions).

R-30.title: More homes allowed by right near jobs
R-30.summary: Homes that meet clear, published rules could be built near jobs and transit without a separate discretionary approval, such as a hearing where neighbors can block each project. Renters and young households would gain within three to ten years as more homes are built and rents ease. Owners in high-demand places would give up some price growth and some control over their neighborhoods.
R-30.effects_confidence: high where binding; medium for US statutes
R-30.remedy_text: Where zoning limits bind, allowing more homes raises building and lowers rents over time. Auckland, New Zealand's 2016 upzoning roughly doubled permits in upzoned areas, and six years later three-bedroom rents were 22% to 35% below a modeled comparison. Minneapolis is also cited, though a 2025 Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis analysis attributes much of that city's slower rent growth to a drop in demand in 2020. Main limitation: results depend on whether zoning was the binding limit, and infrastructure and construction costs can still block delivery.
R-30.what_it_changes: Scarcity raises the value of existing homes (L38: Scarcity raises existing home values), and owners with equity at stake organize to block new supply (L39: Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing). Allowing homes by right moves the decision out of meetings dominated by those owners. The aim is to reduce A5: Housing scarcity and, through it, rents and prices (LE17: Housing scarcity raises rents and prices). The reform works through loop R8 (Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building).

R-31.title: Childcare supply and pay for care workers
R-31.summary: Public money would fund childcare slots and the wages needed to recruit and keep staff, which lowers what families pay and keeps centers open. Parents of young children would gain within two to five years as supply grows. The cost is large and recurring, paid from public budgets.
R-31.remedy_text: Evidence that affordable childcare raises mothers' employment is strong: a 2017 research review found that a 10% drop in cost raises maternal employment by between 0.25% and 11%, a wide range. Evidence on outcomes for children is moderate. Main limitation: quality can suffer when programs grow fast; Quebec's universal program raised maternal employment and was linked to some negative effects on child behavior, a contested finding.
R-31.what_it_changes: Childcare is a major cost for families with young children (EC9: Cost of essentials), and it weighs on A4: Households' financial security. Funding supply together with workforce pay aims to lower prices and keep centers open. It operates on loop R5 (Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions).

R-32.title: Public and philanthropic funding for local news
R-32.summary: Public agencies and foundations would fund reporting on local government, with firewalls that keep funders out of editorial decisions. Residents of counties with little or no local news would gain over years as more reporters cover city halls and school boards. Whether these funds improve accountability has not yet been evaluated.
R-32.remedy_text: Funding models exist. Main limitation: no evaluation has yet shown that these funds improve coverage or accountability, so their effect remains a hypothesis.
R-32.what_it_changes: Platforms took much of the advertising that once paid for local reporting (LT03: Platforms drew ad revenue from local news), and local coverage raises the risk officials face of losing office (L26: Local reporting raises pressure on incumbents). Funding with editorial firewalls aims to restore variable B2: Availability of local reporting, which rises with more reporters and falls as more counties lose their local source. It touches loop R16 (Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other) and loop B1a (Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism).

R-33.title: Citizen assemblies that officials must answer
R-33.summary: A group of residents chosen by lottery to match the makeup of the community would study a hard public question and make recommendations, and officials would have to respond in public. The residents selected would gain a direct role right away. Officials would keep the final decision and would have to explain it.
R-33.remedy_text: Effects on the residents who take part are strong. An OECD review published in 2020 catalogued close to 300 cases of representative deliberation and set out design principles and limits. Main limitation: evidence that assemblies change trust or participation across the wider population is weak.
R-33.what_it_changes: Randomly selected residents deliberate, and officials must answer them publicly. The reform is linked to E2: Trust earned through performance and to variable B3: Civic ties across social and political groups. It sits on loop R9 (Taking part in a successful repair may support the next one), a conceptual loop that remains a hypothesis.

R-34.title: Participatory budgeting: residents decide spending
R-34.summary: Residents would decide how to spend part of a city's budget, proposing projects and voting on them. Neighborhoods with low turnout would gain in the first cycle, and people who take part become more likely to vote in later elections. Council members would give up some discretion over that money.
R-34.remedy_text: In New York City, Johnson, Carlson and Reynolds (2023) found that taking part in participatory budgeting raised participants' later probability of voting by 8.4 percentage points compared with similar voters, with larger effects for young, lower-income and Black voters. Main limitation: the effect is measured among participants, and low participation or a small budget can limit the effect on the wider public.
R-34.what_it_changes: Residents decide part of a budget, which raises later voting among participants. The aim is to raise B5: Equality of voter turnout, where a smaller turnout gap between groups counts as an increase. It sits on loop R9 (Taking part in a successful repair may support the next one), a conceptual loop that remains a hypothesis.

R-35.title: Rejected option: term limits for legislators
R-35.summary: Term limits force experienced legislators out after a set number of terms, and studies of state legislatures find that this weakens how legislatures work. Lobbyists are expected to gain influence once the first legislators reach their limits, an inferred step the studies did not measure.
R-35.remedy_text: Here the grade measures confidence in a finding of harm: strong evidence that term limits weaken legislatures. That finding is the reason the option is rejected, and a strong grade on this page is a warning against adoption. Olson and Rogowski (2020), using state legislative roll-call votes from 1993 to 2016, found that term limits increased polarization, with larger effects in more professional legislatures. Fouirnaies and Hall (2022), studying about 6,000 legislators in states with term limits, found that members who can no longer run again sponsor fewer bills, do less committee work and miss more floor votes. Main limitation: these two studies measure polarization and legislative effort; greater reliance on lobbyists and staff is an inferred mechanism these studies did not measure directly.
R-35.what_it_changes: Term limits remove experienced legislators. The inferred result is that legislatures lean more on lobbyists and staff and produce less. The option sits on the proposed loop R2 (Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise), through L18: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence and L19: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise, and term limits push that loop in the harmful direction.

R-36.title: Lasting public investment in research and infrastructure
R-36.summary: Congress would fund research and infrastructure over several years and protect appropriated money from being canceled or left unspent, so projects reach completion. Future workers and the regions that host research would gain over 10 to 30 years. Current taxpayers would pay now for benefits that arrive later.
R-36.remedy_text: Two studies with different designs find high long-run returns. Fieldhouse and Mertens, in a 2024 working paper, estimate returns of 140% to 210% on nondefense government research, and Gross and Sampat (2023) found that World War II research spending seeded lasting regional clusters of innovation. Main limitation: each study rests on one identification strategy with wide uncertainty, a wartime shock may not generalize, and evidence on delivery is thin.
R-36.what_it_changes: Public research and infrastructure raise private productivity with long lags (LE01: Public research investment raises productivity). Congress appropriates the money (LE02: Congress decides public investment levels), and the executive can withhold, cancel or redirect it (LE03: The executive administers appropriated public investment). Gains depend on money arriving and staying, so delivery and durability matter as much as the size of the budget. The reform sits on no feedback loop.

routes.who: Multi-year appropriations with protection against cancellation
State infrastructure banks and research funds

R-37.title: Feed choice and data access for researchers
R-37.summary: Social media users could choose how their feeds are ranked, and independent researchers could study platform data under privacy safeguards. Users and researchers would gain once the rules take effect, and platforms would lose some control over their data. Experiments show that ranking changes move what people see, with small measured effects on how they feel about the other party.
R-37.remedy_text: Giving users choices shifts what they see, while large experiments found small or no effects on hostility toward the other party. The 2023 X experiment found precisely estimated null effects on partisan hostility, and a 2024 test that reranked hostile posts for 1,256 users of X over ten days moved feelings toward the other party by about 2 points on a 0 to 100 scale. Main limitation: most users keep default settings, so choice alone may change little.
R-37.what_it_changes: Ranking decides what people see (LT01: Engagement-ranked feeds raise hostile-content exposure). The direction of the effect depends on the platform and the ranking rule compared: switching to chronological feeds has raised some kinds of content and lowered others. Concentrated ownership may also entrench engagement ranking (LT02: Platform concentration may entrench engagement ranking, a hypothesis). The reform is a transparency and choice measure acting on loop R3 (Political hostility and hostile content may reinforce each other), whose key link is contested.

routes.who: Platform transparency and researcher access statute

R-38.title: Limits on pricing software using rivals' data
R-38.summary: Software that recommends rents or prices would be barred from using competitors' private data to set live prices. Renters in large buildings would gain within one to three years if the practice has raised rents. Landlords that rely on shared data would lose that advantage.
R-38.remedy_text: The case for the limits rests on design logic. Main limitation: no evaluation of these limits exists yet.
R-38.what_it_changes: Pricing tools fed by competitors' nonpublic data may raise rents (LT12: Shared-data pricing software can raise rents, rated contested). Barring that input removes one channel for coordinated increases through TC7: Use of pricing algorithms. The reform acts on loop R8 (Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building).

R-39.title: Government teams that build digital services
R-39.summary: Government would keep its own teams of technologists to build and run the software people use to claim benefits, get tax refunds and apply for permits. People who use those services would gain within one to three years through faster processing and fewer errors. Large contractors would lose some work.
R-39.remedy_text: Case evidence supports the approach. IRS Direct File, the agency's free online filing tool, accepted 140,803 returns in 2024 and 296,531 in 2025. Main limitation: these are individual cases without a controlled comparison, and teams have not survived changes of administration.
R-39.what_it_changes: Agencies that can build and run their own digital services deliver with fewer failures (LT15: In-house digital teams improve service delivery). Congress funds and can charter that capacity (LT17: Congress decides funding for government digital capacity), while teams created by executive decision can be closed by the next one (LT16: The executive opens and closes federal digital teams). The reform raises TC5: Government's ability to build and run digital services, which feeds D5: Quality of public services. It works through loop R7 (Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other).

routes.who: Statutory charter and protected funding for a digital service

R-40.title: Notice and a voice for workers on AI
R-40.summary: Employers would have to tell workers when AI is used to hire, schedule or evaluate them, explain decisions and offer human review, and negotiate how tools are used where workers have a union. Workers in jobs exposed to AI would gain once the rules are enforced. Employers would bear compliance costs.
R-40.remedy_text: The remedy is a hypothesis. Main limitation: enforcement has been weak where these rules have been tried, as in New York City, so there is little evidence on what working rules would achieve.
R-40.what_it_changes: AI adoption may weaken the position of entry-level workers in exposed jobs (LT05: AI adoption may weaken entry-level workers' position, rated contested). Notice, a way to contest decisions and a say through bargaining aim to protect A2: Workers' bargaining power. The reform operates on loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other).

R-41.title: Large power users pay their grid costs
R-41.summary: Large new electricity users, such as data centers, would pay for the grid capacity and upgrades their demand requires, through rates set by state utility commissions. Households in fast-growing grids would gain at the next rate case, the proceeding in which regulators set a utility's prices. Data-center operators would pay more.
R-41.remedy_text: The case rests on design logic. Main limitation: no evaluation of these tariffs has been found, and loads may move to places offering different terms.
R-41.what_it_changes: Data-center load raises electricity demand and, through capacity prices, household bills (LT11: Data-center load raises household electricity bills, rated plausible). Charging large loads for the costs they cause aims to keep those costs out of EC9: Cost of essentials, and it acts on TC6: Data centers' demand on the electricity grid. The reform sits on no feedback loop.

R-42.title: Congress votes on lasting tariffs
R-42.summary: Tariffs, which are taxes on imports, could stay in place beyond a short period only if Congress voted to approve them. Households and importers would gain when existing tariffs come up for review. Producers protected by tariffs would lose that protection unless Congress chose to keep it.
R-42.remedy_text: The approach is plausible. Learning Resources shows that courts police one statute at a time. Main limitation: no U.S. experience shows how a general vote requirement would work in practice.
R-42.what_it_changes: Presidents now set tariff rates under statutes that delegate the power (LE19: The executive sets tariff rates), and U.S. buyers pay most of the cost (LE18: Tariffs raise prices U.S. buyers pay). Requiring a vote returns a tax power to Congress, the branch the Constitution assigns it to. The reform touches loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).

R-43.title: Building codes and mitigation against disaster losses
R-43.summary: States and cities would adopt and enforce stronger building codes and fund retrofits that reduce damage when storms and other hazards strike. Owners and renters in hazard areas would gain at the next disaster, and insurance would stay more available. Builders would face higher construction costs now.
R-43.remedy_text: The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, a research group supported by property insurers, studied closed claims from Hurricane Charley (2004) in Charlotte County, Florida. Homes built after stricter codes took effect there in 1996 had 40% lower damage frequency and 60% lower damage severity. Main limitation: that study covers one storm in one county, and higher upfront costs and weak enforcement can limit the benefit.
R-43.what_it_changes: Higher hazard raises insurance premiums and nonrenewals (LE20: Climate hazard raises insurance costs), and in high-hazard places insurance costs weigh on home values (LE23: Climate risk weighs on home equity). Stronger codes and mitigation cut losses when hazards hit, which aims to lower EC11: Climate hazards and insurance costs. The reform sits on no feedback loop.

R-44.title: Competition remedies for search and ad markets
R-44.summary: Courts and agencies would impose remedies that open search and online advertising markets to rivals, such as bans on exclusive deals and requirements to share data. Publishers and advertisers would gain over years if the share of ad money captured by a few platforms falls. The dominant platforms would lose some control over these markets.
R-44.remedy_text: Conduct remedies, which regulate a company's behavior without breaking it up, are untested at this scale. Courts found Google liable in search (August 2024) and ad tech (April 2025) and ordered conduct remedies without divestiture, and the FTC lost its case against Meta in November 2025. Main limitation: the market effect depends on the remedy, and some cases remain unresolved.
R-44.what_it_changes: Platforms took the advertising that paid for local reporting (LT03: Platforms drew ad revenue from local news), and concentrated ownership may entrench the goals that govern feeds (LT02: Platform concentration may entrench engagement ranking, a hypothesis). Remedies that open these markets aim to lower TC2: Concentration of platforms and digital advertising. The reform acts on loop R16 (Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other).

R-45.title: Verifiable elections with paper records and audits
R-45.summary: Every vote would leave a paper record, results would be audited, officials would face firm deadlines to certify, and election workers would be protected from threats. Every voter would gain at every election, because results could be checked and accepted. Officials who refuse to certify lawful results would face court orders.
R-45.remedy_text: Evidence is strong that paper records and audits catch errors. A risk-limiting audit, one common design, checks a statistical sample of paper ballots against the reported outcome. Main limitation: audits help only when trained staff run them and officials complete certification lawfully.
R-45.what_it_changes: Paper records, audits and certification on a schedule make results provable, so that C5: Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement can happen and be accepted. Every reform that works through elections rests on this floor. The reform is linked to B5: Equality of voter turnout and to E2: Trust earned through performance, and to loop R4b (Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).

R-46.title: Expand the House of Representatives
R-46.summary: Congress would add seats to the House, so each member would represent fewer people, with a plan for apportionment and staffing. Residents of large states would gain at the next apportionment after the change. A larger chamber could also give party leaders more control.
R-46.remedy_text: Frederick (2010), in observational research, found that larger districts reduce members' contact with constituents and constituents' approval of the member, with modest effects. Main limitation: the effect of expansion on electoral competition is untested.
R-46.what_it_changes: More seats mean smaller districts and more representatives per person, and pairing expansion with multi-member districts (R-03) multiplies the effect. The reform is linked to C1: Seats with little electoral competition and B5: Equality of voter turnout, and to loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates).

R-47.title: Fusion voting and public funding for parties
R-47.summary: More than one party could nominate the same candidate, so a voter could back a candidate on a smaller party's ballot line without splitting the vote. Public funding could also go to parties as well as candidates. Minor parties and their voters would gain in the first election cycle, and major parties would have reason to absorb the smaller lines.
R-47.remedy_text: Experience in New York, where fusion is legal, informs the proposal. Main limitation: evidence comes from few states, and stronger party leaders and absorption of smaller lines are known risks.
R-47.what_it_changes: Fusion voting lets two parties nominate the same candidate, and party-centered funding helps organized coalitions form without spoiling races. The reform is linked to C2: How often the primary decides the winner and C3: Risk of losing office, and to loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates).

R-48.title: Agency independence after the Slaughter ruling
R-48.summary: After the Supreme Court's June 2026 decision in Trump v. Slaughter, Congress would protect independent agencies through other tools: public reasons and records for removals, protected budgets, agency structures the ruling leaves intact, and a written exception for the Federal Reserve. People affected by federal regulation would gain over years if those designs hold. The designs are untested, and their durability depends on how courts apply the decision.
R-48.remedy_text: The proposed designs are untested. Main limitation: their durability depends on how courts apply Slaughter, and no court has yet ruled on designs like these.
R-48.what_it_changes: When officials can be removed at will, watchdogs and regulators weaken (L14: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies), and fewer independent enforcers are left to restrain unilateral action (L15: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action). After Slaughter, independence has to come from structure, such as records, stated reasons for removal, budget protection and the design of lower-level offices, because tenure protection no longer works for many officials. The reform works through loop R18 (Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action).

R-49.title: Civic work that crosses party lines
R-49.summary: Membership groups and service programs would bring people of different parties together for shared work, such as serving as poll workers, again and again over time. Members and their communities would gain on an ongoing basis. Measured drops in hostility tend to fade quickly, so lasting effects across the population are uncertain.
R-49.remedy_text: A 2024 megastudy of 32,059 participants tested 25 interventions: 23 reduced partisan animosity, and the effects faded within about two weeks. A randomized evaluation of Braver Angels workshops at four universities found reduced polarization, with implicit and behavioral effects still present at the study's end (Baron and colleagues, 2025). Main limitation: most effects decay, and lasting change across the population is unmeasured.
R-49.what_it_changes: Ties formed through shared work across party lines can reduce hostility (L33: Cross-group ties reduce partisan hostility, rated plausible) and make turnout more equal (L34: Civic ties make turnout more equal, rated well-supported). The reform builds variable B3: Civic ties across social and political groups and operates on loop R15 (Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other).

R-50.title: Popular-vote compact and constitutional amendment options
R-50.summary: R-50 covers long-term options for how senators and presidents are chosen: constitutional amendments on Senate apportionment and the Electoral College, and the National Popular Vote compact, which needs no amendment. Under the compact, member states would award their electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner once states holding 270 electoral votes have joined. Voters in states that are not competitive in presidential races would gain if it takes effect.
R-50.remedy_text: The compact is untested, and no court has ruled on it. Main limitation: it has not taken effect, so neither its legal standing nor its effects on campaigns are known.
R-50.what_it_changes: A durable Senate majority shapes the courts over decades, and Senate malapportionment, the unequal populations of states that each have two senators, is a fixed feature of that link (L57: Durable Senate majorities shape court appointments). These options act on D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions and D3: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition, and on loop R12 (Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules).

glossary.Absolute mobility: Whether children grow up to have higher income than their parents had at a similar age, after adjusting for inflation.
glossary.Affective polarization: Hostility toward people in the other political party. Studies measure it separately from disagreement over policy.
glossary.Association: Two measures that move together without an established causal path. The Atlas keeps associations in the register and never draws them on a map.
glossary.Authority connection: A connection showing that one body holds legal power over something: it appoints, appropriates, preempts, enforces or sets a rate. It says who decides, without saying which way the decision goes, so it has no sign and never closes a loop.
glossary.Balancing loop (B): A feedback loop whose response pushes back against the first change. How well it works depends on whether each corrective step can act.
glossary.By-right development: Building that can go ahead when it meets published rules, without a separate discretionary approval for that project.
glossary.Causal connection: A connection stating that a change in one variable changes another in a stated direction, other things held equal. It carries a sign, a delay and an evidence grade.
glossary.Cloture: A Senate vote to end debate. For most legislation it takes 60 votes, which is how the filibuster blocks bills that have majority support.
glossary.Conditional direction: A judgment of which way an outcome could move if stated requirements hold. It gives no numerical size and no forecast.
glossary.Confidence label: The short label on a claim or response saying what kind of evidence supports it: documented, well-supported, plausible, contested, hypothesis or not yet tested. The same scale grades connections on the map.
glossary.Connection: A claimed relationship between two variables. Its record explains the mechanism, gives the evidence grade and states the delay. Connection IDs begin with L, LE, LT, LX or T.
glossary.Continuing resolution: A temporary law that keeps agencies funded at existing levels when Congress has not passed regular appropriations, which prevents a shutdown.
glossary.Counterevidence: Evidence that challenges a claim, narrows its scope or supports another explanation.
glossary.Counterfactual: An estimate of what would have happened without the change being studied, used as the comparison for measuring an effect.
glossary.Delay: The time between a change and its effect. Codes: S, under 2 years; M, 2 to 10 years; L, over 10 years.
glossary.Delivery log: A list of 24 times American government did something hard at scale, each with its measured result, who enacted it and the qualification that travels with the result.
glossary.Democracy: A system in which people can choose and replace leaders through meaningful elections, with equal political standing, civil liberties and enforceable limits on power. Measures of democracy combine these elements in different ways.
glossary.Derived quantity: A variable calculated from others, such as how often the primary decides the winner. Drawn as a box with a thin border.
glossary.Distribution overlay: A lens showing how the same rule or connection reaches a group differently, through a named mechanism. Groups stay outside the variables, because a group cannot rise or fall as a quantity in a loop.
glossary.Documented: The confidence label for a fact or event on the public record: a statute, a court ruling or an official statistic. It establishes the event; it says nothing about the size of an effect unless the record does.
glossary.Durability: How well a change survives a new legislature, a new administration, a court challenge or a loss of funding.
glossary.Effect code: A code showing the expected direction and rough size of a reform's effect on an outcome family: +L large positive, +M moderate positive, +S small positive, 0 no expected effect, -S small negative, -M moderate negative, ? direction uncertain.
glossary.Electoral pressure: The credible chance that an official will lose office. It can change behavior before any election removes anyone.
glossary.Entry document: An ordinary paper a reader already handles, such as a rent renewal, a pay stub, a primary ballot, a bill or a notice, used as a starting point into the map.
glossary.Feasibility: A judgment of whether a route to change is open under present political and legal conditions. The Atlas rates it high, medium, low or very low for 2026 to 2030.
glossary.Feedback loop: A chain of causes that returns to its starting variable. Reinforcing loops amplify change and balancing loops counteract it; either kind can produce good or harmful results.
glossary.Flow: An amount arriving or leaving over a period, such as annual income or money spent per election cycle. Its time unit is part of the measure.
glossary.Fusion voting: A rule letting one candidate appear on the ballot lines of more than one party. It is legal and in regular use in New York and Connecticut.
glossary.Hold threshold: For each outcome indicator, the 2036 level below which conditions would be getting worse. It is a teaching benchmark and makes no forecast.
glossary.Hypothesis: The confidence label for a proposed relationship that needs stronger evidence. Diagrams draw it as a dotted line, and it never serves as the only support for a claim.
glossary.Impoundment: A President's withholding of money Congress has appropriated. The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 makes it unlawful unless Congress approves a rescission.
glossary.Income: Money and resources received over a period. A figure should say whether it is for a household or a person, whether it is before or after taxes and benefits, and how it adjusts for inflation.
glossary.Indicator: A dated measurement used to track a variable, with a defined population and source. An indicator can capture its variable imperfectly; survey trust, for example, only partly tracks trust earned through performance.
glossary.Information connection: A connection along which content, data or attention moves, such as news coverage, feeds or disclosure. Its sign gives the causal effect on the target.
glossary.Inspector general: An official inside a federal agency who audits and investigates it. The law requires 30 days' notice to Congress and a specific reason before the President removes one.
glossary.Issue record: One of 193 records beneath the map, with IDs such as I017 or X01. Each describes a documented problem, case or policy, names its mechanism, gives an evidence grade, status and sources, and links to a variable or connection where it can.
glossary.Jurisdiction: The place or governing body to which a rule, study or claim applies.
glossary.Labor share: The part of income from production paid to workers as compensation. Its exact scope depends on the statistical series.
glossary.Leverage point: A place in a system where a change has wide effects. The Atlas ranks seven for teaching, using Donella Meadows' ordering from changing a number (low reach) to changing a system's goals (high reach).
glossary.Loop closure: A complete path of connections that returns to the starting variable. If any closing step is only a hypothesis, the whole loop stays uncertain.
glossary.Market power: The ability to profitably worsen prices or terms because customers, workers or suppliers lack good alternatives. National concentration alone does not measure it.
glossary.Mechanism: The steps through which one change produces another.
glossary.Mid-decade redistricting: Redrawing election districts between the once-a-decade redraws that follow each census.
glossary.Money connection: A connection along which dollars move, such as contributions, advertising revenue, taxes, transfers or prices. Its sign gives the causal effect of that movement on the target.
glossary.Mutually exclusive and collectively exha: A way of sorting in which every item fits in one category only and the categories together cover everything within a stated boundary. Each issue has one main category, while its causes and effects can cross many.
glossary.Negative sign (−): The connected variables tend to move in opposite directions, with the model's other conditions held steady.
glossary.Outcome family: One of four groups of results used to judge reforms: democratic quality, government efficacy, economic performance, and income and wealth equality. The families use different units and are never added together.
glossary.Outside driver: A force that affects the model but whose own causes lie outside its boundary, such as technology, population patterns, trade, foreign interference and major shocks. Drawn as a rounded pill outside the clusters.
glossary.Ownership connection: A connection where one quantity is held inside another or holds claims on it, such as stock holdings inside household wealth. Its sign says how a change in the part moves the whole.
glossary.Pathway: A guided answer to one everyday question, such as why rent went up. It gives a short answer, the main mechanisms, narrower questions, the offices that decide, possible responses and the evidence behind each claim.
glossary.Plausible: The confidence label for a coherent mechanism with some supporting evidence, where the studies are weak or few.
glossary.Contested: The confidence label for a relationship on which credible studies disagree. Both sides are shown with the connection.
glossary.Positive sign (+): The connected variables tend to move in the same direction, with the model's other conditions held steady. A positive sign does not mean a benefit.
glossary.Preclearance: The Voting Rights Act requirement that places with a history of discrimination get federal approval before changing voting rules. It stopped operating after Shelby County v. Holder (2013).
glossary.Preemption: A higher level of government limiting what a lower level may do on a subject, such as a state barring cities from adopting ranked-choice voting.
glossary.Problem evidence: Evidence that the condition or mechanism a reform addresses exists. It is graded separately from remedy evidence.
glossary.Quorum: The minimum number of members a body needs to take certain actions. An agency can exist while lacking the quorum it needs to act.
glossary.Ranked-choice voting: A method in which voters rank candidates; if no one wins a majority of first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots move to their next choice until someone wins.
glossary.Reconciliation: A federal budget procedure that lets qualifying tax and spending legislation pass the Senate by simple majority. Its rules limit what it can carry, and most rule changes fall outside it.
glossary.Reference mode: An observed pattern over time that the model is meant to explain, such as the rise in the top 1% share of wealth.
glossary.Reform profile: One of 50 entries, R-01 to R-50, describing a proposed change: the connections it aims at, the routes it can travel, what it depends on, separate evidence about the problem and the remedy, expected directions for each outcome family, and how it could fail.
glossary.Reinforcing loop (R): A feedback loop whose returning effect amplifies the first change. Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.
glossary.Rejected connection: A relationship that was reviewed against the evidence and left off the map, kept on record with the reason, such as the claim that feed ranking alone raises hostility toward the other party.
glossary.Relative mobility: How strongly a person's place in the income distribution depends on family background. Everyone cannot rise in relative rank at the same time.
glossary.Remedy evidence: Evidence that an intervention changes the condition it targets, with attention to where and how it was carried out.
glossary.Repair log: A dated list of 64 rule changes that altered who officials answer to, coded toward voters, away from voters, voters kept existing rules, mixed or pending.
glossary.Route: A path a reform can travel through government or civil society, such as a city ordinance, a state statute, a ballot measure, a federal statute, executive action, a court ruling or a constitutional amendment. The Atlas uses eleven routes.
glossary.Safe seat: A seat where one party or candidate has a large expected advantage. The model counts seats won by more than ten points; check each source's definition before comparing counts.
glossary.Sanction applied: An electoral loss, or a retirement under threat of defeat, that removes an official. The model separates this event from the earlier risk of losing.
glossary.Scenario: A set of stated assumptions with the direction each outcome family would take if they hold. Scenarios are conditional directions, never forecasts or odds.
glossary.Snapshot: The dated state of the research behind the Atlas, most recently October 15, 2026. Facts that were checked carry their own check date; inclusion in the snapshot alone does not mean a fact was rechecked on that date.
glossary.Source: A citable item with its publisher, date, link, study design and limitations.
glossary.Source register: The list of every source the Atlas cites. Each entry has an ID (a letter, S, N, Q, W or K, followed by numbers), title, publisher, date and link, with notes on the study design, its limits and how it was read.
glossary.State capacity: Government's lawful ability to gather information, decide, carry out decisions, enforce rules and learn. Capacity and accountability need to be designed together.
glossary.Stock: An amount built up over time, such as wealth, debt, local news outlets or safe seats. It changes only through what flows in and out.
glossary.Success threshold: For each outcome indicator, the 2036 level that would mark a clear improvement. It is a teaching benchmark and makes no forecast.
glossary.Supplemental Poverty Measure: A Census Bureau poverty measure that counts taxes, tax credits and benefits such as food aid, and subtracts costs such as medical expenses, so it can show how much a program reduces poverty.
glossary.Top-two and top-four primaries: Primaries in which every candidate appears on one ballot and the top two (or four) finishers advance to the general election, whatever their party.
glossary.Topic: One of five groups of pathways built around a part of everyday life: cost of living; health and care; work and financial security; public services where you live; and voice, power and information.
glossary.Variable: A quantity or condition in the model that can rise or fall. Its definition states what a higher or lower value means.
glossary.Warranted trust: Confidence that follows shown competence, honesty and accountability, as distinct from unconditional trust in whoever holds office.
glossary.Wealth (net worth): Assets minus debts at a point in time. A rise in an asset's value that has not been sold is different from cash income or taxable income.
glossary.Well-supported: The confidence label for a relationship on which several credible studies, designed to rule out other explanations, agree about direction. Each study's setting and limits still apply.
